title: Scalar User-defined functions (UDFs) in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Generally Available)
author: SMATIN

content.text:
T-SQL scalar user-defined functions (UDFs) are now generally available in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint.
During preview, scalar UDFs gained support for procedural T-SQL and additional query shapes through Expression Block inlining, a technology built to run procedural logic at warehouse scale. A subsequent preview update expanded loop control, large-value data type support, and the query shapes available to scalar UDFs.
General availability builds on that foundation with time-dependent functions, AT TIME ZONE, NEWID(), and improved resource estimation for control-flow statements.
Data teams can keep time-sensitive and identifier-generation rules in reusable T-SQL rather than duplicating them across application code, orchestration steps, or queries. The authoring model remains unchanged: existing definitions, permissions, catalog metadata, and call syntax continue to apply.
What’s new
This release adds the following capabilities:
Area
New capability
What it enables
Expression Block inlining
Time-dependent functions including GETDATE(), GETUTCDATE(), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, SYSDATETIME(), SYSUTCDATETIME(), and SYSDATETIMEOFFSET()
Time-aware procedural rules across analytical query shapes
Expression Block inlining and Scalar UDF inlining
AT TIME ZONE
Reusable regional and business-time conversion
Expression Block inlining
NEWID()
A new identifier for each evaluated output row
Query resource estimation
Improved estimation for conditional and iterative work
Resource allocation that more closely reflects expected control-flow work
You use the same T-SQL syntax for every scalar UDF. Fabric determines the applicable inlining technique from the function definition.
Use current time in procedural business rules
Many business rules depend on when a query runs. Examples include SLA classification, expiration checks, processing windows, aging bands, and effective-date logic.
Expression Block inlining now supports time-dependent functions inside scalar UDF bodies. The following function compares an order's creation time with the current UTC time and returns its SLA state:
CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION dbo.fn_GetOrderSlaState
(
@CreatedUtc DATETIME2(6),
@TargetMinutes INT
)
RETURNS VARCHAR(20)
AS
BEGIN
DECLARE @CurrentUtc DATETIME2(6) = SYSUTCDATETIME();
DECLARE @TargetUtc DATETIME2(6) = DATEADD(MINUTE, @TargetMinutes, @CreatedUtc);
IF @CreatedUtc > @CurrentUtc
RETURN 'Not started';
IF @CurrentUtc <= @TargetUtc
RETURN 'Within target';
RETURN 'Past target';
END;
Use the function to summarize orders by their current SLA state:
WITH OrderSlaStates AS
(
SELECT
OrderId,
dbo.fn_GetOrderSlaState(CreatedUtc, TargetMinutes) AS SlaState
FROM dbo.OrderProcessing
)
SELECT
SlaState,
COUNT_BIG(*) AS OrderCount
FROM OrderSlaStates
GROUP BY SlaState
ORDER BY SlaState;
The time expression is evaluated during query processing. Separate evaluations can observe different clock values, while multiple rows can receive the same value because of clock resolution and execution timing. Use time-dependent functions for time-aware logic, not as a source of unique row identifiers.
The same behavior applies when the function is called from supported CTEs, filters, joins, and grouping queries. The rule remains defined once even when different analytical queries consume it.
Apply time-zone rules inside scalar UDFs
Operational data is frequently stored in UTC but interpreted according to a business or regional time zone. Keeping the conversion in a function avoids duplicating chained AT TIME ZONE expressions across ingestion, reporting, and monitoring queries.
Both Expression Block inlining and Scalar UDF inlining now support AT TIME ZONE. The following example showcases the Expression Block path by converting a supplied UTC value to Eastern time:
CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION dbo.fn_ToEasternTime
(
@UtcValue DATETIME2(6)
)
RETURNS DATETIMEOFFSET(6)
AS
BEGIN
DECLARE @EasternValue DATETIMEOFFSET(6);
SET @EasternValue = @UtcValue
AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'
AT TIME ZONE 'Eastern Standard Time';
RETURN @EasternValue;
END;
Because Expression Block inlining applies to this definition, the function can be used in the various query shapes supported by that technique. This CTE converts each stored UTC value before the outer query consumes it:
WITH LocalOrderTimes AS
(
SELECT
OrderId,
CreatedUtc,
dbo.fn_ToEasternTime(CreatedUtc) AS EasternCreatedTime
FROM dbo.OrderProcessing
)
SELECT
OrderId,
CreatedUtc,
EasternCreatedTime
FROM LocalOrderTimes
ORDER BY OrderId;
The function returns the same DATETIMEOFFSET value as the equivalent direct expression and applies the daylight-saving-time rules associated with the selected Windows time-zone name.
Functions using Scalar UDF inlining can use the same clause within that technique's supported function bodies and calling-query shapes. Supporting the clause through both techniques avoids requiring a separate time-zone conversion strategy when a function follows a different inlining path.
Generate identifiers for output rows
Expression Block inlining now supports NEWID() inside a scalar UDF body. This supports reusable identifier-generation logic that produces a new value for each evaluated output row.
CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION dbo.fn_NewProcessingId()
RETURNS UNIQUEIDENTIFIER
AS
BEGIN
RETURN NEWID();
END;
When the function is evaluated over a row set, each row receives a new value:
SELECT
OrderId,
dbo.fn_NewProcessingId() AS ProcessingId
FROM dbo.OrderProcessing
ORDER BY OrderId;
If an executed function path contains multiple NEWID() calls, each evaluated call produces a separate value. Normal variable semantics still apply, assigning NEWID() to a local variable performs one evaluation, while reading that variable again reuses the stored value.
NEWID() is evaluated for each output row, including across distributed execution nodes.
Match resource estimates to control-flow work
Procedural functions can perform different amounts of work depending on their conditional paths and loop iterations. A compact function call does not necessarily represent a small amount of computation.
Resource estimation for scalar UDF control flow has improved. The query optimizer can better account for the work represented by conditional paths and loop iterations when determining the resources required by a workload. Existing functions and calling queries receive this improvement without hints or code changes.
What's next
No hints or syntax changes are required. Existing UDFs gain newly supported capabilities automatically.
For current syntax, metadata, and the construct support for each inlining technique, refer to CREATE FUNCTION for Fabric Data Warehouse. For a guided introduction, refer to Create scalar user-defined functions in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse.
Thank you to the customers and partners who used scalar UDFs during preview and shared scenarios and feedback with us. We welcome additional scenarios and feedback at Fabric DW functions feedback.
